sections.heading: How to use PlayGarba.
sections.text: Open the player, choose a Garba style and press play. Explore and Nonstop are there when you need them.

sections.heading: Three things to know.
sections.text: The player is designed to stay understandable without a tutorial.

sections.text: Use playgarba.com for listening.

sections.text: Traditional, Dandiya, Devotional, Folk, Sanedo or Fusion.

sections.heading: Play or explore.
sections.text: Stay with the current music, search the catalogue or open Nonstop.

sections.heading: Use the live address for listening.
sections.text: playgarba.com is the player. Bookmark it or install it if you want a home-screen or desktop icon. For the simple listening handoff page, use PlayGarba Live. Direct listening still starts at playgarba.com.

sections.heading: Search when you know what you want.
sections.text: Explore opens the catalogue. Search by song or artist, then use the catalogue views to move through releases and Garba categories.

sections.heading: The important controls stay close to the music.
sections.text: Use play and pause, previous and next, favourites, share and queue where those controls are available for the current listening state.

sections.heading: Use Nonstop for longer sets.
sections.text: Nonstop is for continuous Garba releases and longer performances. It uses the same player, so you can move in and out without learning another interface.

sections.heading: Playback comes from YouTube.
sections.text: PlayGarba uses verified YouTube routes for playback. The video stays collapsed unless you choose to open it. If a catalogue item does not yet have a verified YouTube route, it can remain unavailable until that route is added.

sections.heading: Listen with friends.
sections.text: Private Garba Circle plays the same song at the same moment on everyone's phone. It works for a silent garba with earbuds, or for friends in different places. Tap Private Garba Circle above 24/7 LIVE, or Circle in the Immersive rail, then share the link or QR code. Only people with the link can join. Choose Keep the music going to play the catalogue in one shared order, or Play your songs to play this song, your Up next and any YouTube links you paste. As the host you can keep adding songs; share the new link so everyone hears them.

sections.heading: Start here.

No. The video is kept collapsed by default and can be opened from the YouTube control when you want to see it. Why might a catalogue item be unavailable? sections.heading: Home screen and desktop.

What should I do if the player looks stale? Reconnect to the internet and reopen or refresh the live player. Found a bug or a missing song? Open the GitHub issues page

sections.text: You can use PlayGarba in any supported browser. Installing it simply gives the live player its own home-screen or desktop icon.

sections.heading: Install with Safari
sections.text: Use Brave for background listening. To add a PlayGarba icon to your Home Screen, use Safari: Open playgarba.com in Safari. Tap Share. Choose Add to Home Screen. On iPhone, if it is missing, scroll down, tap Edit Actions, then add Add to Home Screen. Turn on Open as Web App. Tap Add.

sections.text: Install from Brave to add PlayGarba to your home screen, then use Brave for background listening. Open playgarba.com in Brave. Open the Brave menu beside the address bar. Tap Install app or Add to Home screen. Confirm, then open PlayGarba from its new home-screen icon.

sections.heading: Install from your browser
sections.text: Open playgarba.com. Use the Install control in the address bar or choose the app-install option from the menu. Confirm the installation. Open playgarba.com. Choose Settings and more More tools Apps Install this site as an app. Confirm the installation. Open playgarba.com in Safari. Choose File Add to Dock. Confirm the addition.

sections.heading: Keep the Garba going in Brave.
sections.text: PlayGarba streams songs from YouTube. Brave 1.87 and newer includes improved YouTube background playback and picture-in-picture on Android and iPhone/iPad, with media controls available from the lock screen. Install or update Brave from Google Play for Android or the App Store for iPhone and iPad. Open playgarba.com in Brave and press Play. Wait for the song to start. Leave the PlayGarba tab open. Switch to another app or lock your phone. If the song pauses, open the lock-screen or notification media controls and press Play. Return to the Brave tab and press Play again if the controls are not available. If it still stops, update Brave to version 1.87 or newer, reopen PlayGarba in Brave, and…

sections.text: On Mac, Windows and Linux, playback usually continues when you switch to another tab or app. If it pauses, return to PlayGarba and press Play.

sections.text: The installed version opens the same PlayGarba player in a standalone app-style window where your browser supports it.

sections.heading: Remove it like another home-screen or desktop app.

sections.page: What is Garba? The circle, centre and Navratri tradition
sections.heading: What is Garba?
sections.text: Garba is a ritual and devotional dance from Gujarat, performed during Navratri. Dancers move around a lit earthen pot or an image of Amba, singing and clapping as the circle moves together.

sections.page: What is Garba? The circle, centre and Navratri tradition
sections.heading: Begin with Amba or the light.
sections.text: The circle is organised around a devotional centre during Navratri.

sections.page: What is Garba? The circle, centre and Navratri tradition
sections.heading: Movement, singing and clapping.
sections.text: Dancers move together around the centre while the rhythm builds.

sections.page: What is Garba? The circle, centre and Navratri tradition
sections.heading: A practice carried by people.
sections.text: Dancers, musicians, craftspeople and others pass Garba across generations.

sections.page: What is Garba? The circle, centre and Navratri tradition
sections.heading: Garba starts with a devotional centre.
sections.text: Navratri is dedicated to the worship of feminine energy, or Shakti. UNESCO describes Garba taking place around either an image of the mother goddess Amba or a perforated earthenware pot lit with an oil lamp. The lit pot is one recognised form of that centre, not a required prop in every Garba. The important point is that the dancers are moving around a shared devotional focus.

sections.page: What is Garba? The circle, centre and Navratri tradition
sections.heading: The dance is built around collective movement.
sections.text: UNESCO describes dancers moving around the centre in a counter-clockwise circle, using simple movements while singing and clapping in unison. The tempo can build from slower circular movement into faster whirling. Seen this way, the circle is not just a formation. It connects the devotional centre, the group and the rhythm.

sections.page: What is Garba? The circle, centre and Navratri tradition
sections.heading: Garba is more than the people dancing.
sections.text: UNESCO identifies a broad community around Garba, including dancers, musicians, social groups, craftspeople and religious figures involved in the festivities and preparations. The practice is transmitted in rural and urban areas through practice, performance, imitation and observation. Garba continues because people take part in it and pass it on.

sections.page: What is Garba? The circle, centre and Navratri tradition
sections.heading: They can share a Navratri night without being the same dance.
sections.text: Garba centres on collective circular movement around the devotional centre and commonly uses clapping as part of the movement. Dandiya is used for forms of Raas in which dancers use small wooden sticks as part of the rhythm and choreography. PlayGarba keeps Garba and Dandiya/Raas distinct rather than using the names interchangeably.

sections.page: What is Garba? The circle, centre and Navratri tradition
sections.heading: The music serves different forms of movement and listening.
sections.text: Navratri gatherings can move through sung Garba, instrumental accompaniment and Raas/Dandiya music. PlayGarba keeps Traditional, Dandiya, Devotional, Folk, Sanedo and Fusion as separate ways into the catalogue so those differences remain visible. Use Traditional for the core Garba collection, Dandiya for Raas-led listening, Devotional for worship-centred listening, or Nonstop for longer continuous recordings and sets. These are listening routes, not rankings.

sections.page: What is Garba? The circle, centre and Navratri tradition
sections.heading: Garba of Gujarat was inscribed in 2023.
sections.text: UNESCO inscribed Garba of Gujarat on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2023.

sections.heading: The setting changes. The practice continues.
sections.text: Garba is carried across generations through Navratri devotion, circular movement, music, craft and participation. Rural and urban settings can differ, but the practice is learned by taking part.

sections.heading: A devotional centre and a circle.
sections.text: Navratri, Amba or the lit earthen pot, movement, singing and clapping remain central reference points.

sections.heading: People learn by taking part.
sections.text: Practice, performance, imitation and observation carry Garba across generations.

sections.heading: Place, scale and presentation.
sections.text: A living tradition can appear in different settings without becoming one fixed stage format.

sections.heading: Start with the centre and the circle.
sections.text: UNESCO describes Garba as a ritualistic and devotional dance performed during Navratri, around a lit earthenware pot or an image of the mother goddess Amba. Dancers move around the centre while singing and clapping in unison. This gives a useful foundation for understanding Garba over time. The practice is not defined by one singer, one venue or one modern event format. Its identity is carried through collective participation around a devotional centre.

sections.heading: Garba is learned by doing it with other people.
sections.text: UNESCO says Garba is transmitted in rural and urban areas through practice, performance, imitation and observation. That means continuity does not depend on freezing one version of the dance in time. People watch, join, learn, perform and teach. The practice continues because it remains active rather than becoming only an object of historical study.

sections.heading: Continuity does not require every Garba to look the same.
sections.text: Garba is practised in both rural and urban settings. Contemporary gatherings may use larger grounds, amplification, recorded music, newer arrangements and changing dress alongside older community practices. The useful question is not simply whether a setting looks old or new. It is whether the devotional centre, collective movement, music and community context remain understandable rather than being reduced to generic festival imagery.

sections.heading: The tradition includes more than dancers.
sections.text: UNESCO describes the practitioners and bearers of Garba broadly, including dancers, musicians, social groups, craftspeople and religious figures involved in the festivities and preparations. This wider view connects music, pottery, clothing, ornaments, dance and organisation. It also explains why PlayGarba's cultural pages separate the listening experience from the evidence-backed context around it.

sections.heading: Garba of Gujarat entered UNESCO's Representative List in 2023.
sections.text: UNESCO inscribed Garba of Gujarat on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2023, recognising it as living heritage carried by communities and transmitted across generations.

sections.heading: The song and the circle move together.
sections.text: Garba music is built for collective movement, with singing, clapping, percussion and tempo working together.

sections.heading: The music is designed to be moved to together.
sections.text: UNESCO's description of Garba places singing and clapping inside the dance itself. Dancers move around the centre while singing and clapping in unison, so rhythm is not something delivered only from a stage. The group helps create it. That relationship is one reason Garba can feel different from music made mainly for passive listening. Repetition, pulse and clear rhythmic phrasing help a large circle stay together.

sections.heading: The energy can build as the dance develops.
sections.text: UNESCO describes Garba beginning with simpler circular movements and the tempo building toward faster whirling. Not every modern recording follows one fixed progression, but increasing energy remains a familiar feature of live Garba. Longer Nonstop sets can make that progression especially clear because the musical flow continues across an extended performance.

sections.heading: Voice, clapping and percussion carry the pulse.
sections.text: Official tourism descriptions of contemporary Navratri celebrations refer to rhythmic dhol beats alongside singing, clapping and Dandiya sticks. Instrumentation varies by artist, ensemble, period and setting, so there is no single mandatory modern Garba arrangement. The useful constant is function: the music supports a shared dance rhythm.

sections.heading: Garba music keeps absorbing new arrangements.
sections.text: UNESCO's inscription notes that generations redefine Garba through new performing styles and lyrics. That helps explain why traditional, devotional, folk-led and contemporary arrangements can all sit inside the broader Garba catalogue. PlayGarba keeps those listening contexts visible instead of flattening every recording into one generic Garba label.

sections.heading: The sticks are part of the dance, not decoration.
sections.text: Dandiya Raas is a Gujarati group dance built around paired wooden sticks, circular movement and rhythmic exchange.

sections.heading: Dandiya creates rhythm through contact.
sections.text: Gujarat Tourism describes Dandiya Raas as a circular group dance performed with small wooden sticks. Dancers strike their own or a partner's sticks as they move, turning the sticks into part of both the choreography and the audible rhythm. This is the quickest practical clue for identifying Dandiya Raas. If the dance is organised around paired sticks, you are looking at a Raas form rather than ordinary Garba clapping.

sections.heading: It belongs to a broader Gujarati Raas tradition.
sections.text: Official Gujarat tourism material connects Raas traditions particularly with Saurashtra and Kutch and with Krishna and Gop cultural references. Modern Navratri programmes may present Dandiya Raas alongside Garba, but its movement vocabulary and cultural references remain distinct.

sections.heading: The pattern depends on timing with other dancers.
sections.text: The sticks make coordination visible and audible. Dancers move through repeating patterns, meeting partners or lines at the correct beat. Different events and communities use different steps, so there is no single universal Dandiya sequence. 04 · GARBA +

sections.heading: They share Navratri nights, not one identity.
sections.text: Large Navratri gatherings often move between Garba and Dandiya Raas. That is why the words are sometimes used loosely for the same evening. PlayGarba keeps Dandiya as a distinct listening category in Explore, so the distinction does not disappear inside the catalogue.

sections.heading: Same festival night. Different dance forms.
sections.text: Garba and Dandiya are often grouped together during Navratri, but the movement, objects and cultural references are different.

sections.heading: Garba centres the circle, clapping and devotion.
sections.text: UNESCO describes Garba as a ritualistic and devotional dance performed during Navratri. Dancers move in a circle around a lit earthen pot or an image of the mother goddess Amba, singing and clapping in unison. In that description, the defining elements are the ritual centre, circular movement, shared rhythm and devotion.

sections.heading: Dandiya adds paired sticks and a different Raas tradition.
sections.text: Gujarat Tourism distinguishes Dandiya Raas from Garba and describes it as a circular group dance using small wooden sticks. Its cultural references are associated with Krishna and Gop traditions, particularly in Saurashtra and Kutch. The sticks are not simply Garba props. They are part of what makes Dandiya Raas a distinct form.

sections.heading: Modern Navratri events often programme both.
sections.text: A single night can move between Garba and Dandiya Raas, so everyday conversation often uses “Garba” as a broad label for the whole dance event. That is understandable in practice, but it can blur the distinction between the forms. On PlayGarba, Dandiya remains a distinct listening category inside Explore so the musical and cultural distinction stays visible.

sections.heading: Garba uses the circle and clapping. Dandiya Raas uses sticks.
sections.text: That is the simplest practical distinction. The deeper difference is that Garba is closely tied to the Navratri worship of Shakti, while Dandiya Raas carries its own Raas and Krishna-linked traditions.

sections.heading: Nine nights. One circle around Shakti.
sections.text: In Gujarat, Garba is one of the defining ways communities gather during Navratri.

sections.heading: Navratri literally means “nine nights”.
sections.text: Navratri is celebrated in many parts of India, but Gujarat is especially associated with nine nights of public and community dance. Gujarat Tourism describes villages and cities gathering in open spaces throughout the state during the festival. Garba is not an entertainment layer added to Navratri. Its devotional meaning is part of why the dance belongs to the festival.

sections.heading: The festival centres feminine divinity.
sections.text: UNESCO describes Garba as being performed during Navratri, a festival dedicated to the worship of feminine energy, or Shakti. The mother goddess Amba is one of the central devotional references within the Garba tradition.

sections.heading: The centre of the circle is meaningful.
sections.text: A traditional Garba circle may form around a perforated earthenware pot illuminated by an oil lamp, or around an image of the mother goddess. Gujarat Tourism also describes a community shrine and garbo as a focal point of the festival. This is why the visual language of a circle around a lit centre appears so often in descriptions of Garba. It reflects the structure of the practice itself.

sections.heading: The festival is carried by more than dancers.
sections.text: UNESCO identifies dancers, musicians, social groups, craftspeople and religious figures among the practitioners and bearers of Garba. Public events may be large, but the tradition also continues through neighbourhoods, families, villages and smaller community gatherings. The shared night is part of the tradition: people gather, sing, clap, dance, prepare spaces, make garments and ornaments, and pass the practice on by participation.

sections.heading: Garba is made as well as danced.
sections.text: Clothing, ornaments, pottery and other craft traditions help give Garba its material identity.

sections.heading: Garba's cultural system includes craftspeople.
sections.text: UNESCO identifies craftspeople among the practitioners and bearers who sustain Garba. Its safeguarding material specifically refers to costume-making and pottery alongside music and dance. That means the visual identity of Garba is not separate from the tradition. It is made by people whose work supports the gatherings themselves.

sections.heading: There is no single permanent Garba uniform.
sections.text: Garba clothing varies by region, community, event and period. Embroidery, mirror work, textile colour and movement-friendly silhouettes are common visual associations, but styles continue to change. For a cultural guide, it is safer to recognise that range than to claim one outfit is the only authentic way to dress for Garba. 03 · ORNAMENTS +

sections.heading: Dress sits beside pottery and festival objects.
sections.text: UNESCO's description links the Garba ecosystem with garments, ornaments and the making of the garbha-deep. Together, these objects make the festival visible as well as audible. That is why PlayGarba's approved image library includes craftspeople, textiles, instruments and ritual objects rather than only dancers on a stage.

sections.heading: New dress can still belong to a living tradition.
sections.text: UNESCO noted during inscription that every generation redefines Garba through new performing styles, lyrics and dress while retaining its cultural centre. Clothing changes are therefore part of the documented evolution of the form.
